title: Troubleshooting biGBac: a practical guide
author: Erin Cutts

steps_raw.instruction: Troubleshooting	biGBac:	a	practical	guide	Erin	Cutts	and	Alessandro	Vannini	The	Institute	of	Cancer	Research,	London,	SW7	3RP,	UK Abstract	The biGBac	system	p r e s e n t e d b y Weissmann	et al.	(Weissmann	et al,	2016	and	Weissmann	et	al,	2018)	is	a	modular	insect	cell	expression	system	designed	for expression of multi-subunit complexes.	T h e system is very powerful,	allowing up to 25 genes	to be assembled into one baculo-virus expression	vector,	but	does	require	a	reasonable	amount	of	cloning	experience	in	order	to	attain	clones	in	the	6	day	time	frame	stated	in	the	paper.	This	guide	was	written	to provide a detailed explanation how the system is designed,	how it can be	further	exploited	and	provide	in-depth	practical	information	that	even	a	novice	cloner	can	follow. Introduction	The	Design	of	the	System	The biGBac system uses the Gibson assembly method,	where	homologous	double-stranded regions and a cocktail of enzymes	are used	to join multiple	DNA fragments together (Gibson	et al,	2009).	There are many online guides to	how this works and many	different versions of Gibson assembly enzyme mix	available commercially.	In brief, the assembly mix contains an exonuclease, a	polymerase	and	a	ligase.	On	incubating	the	DNA	fragments	with	assembly	mix	at	50°C, the exonuclease	c h e w s	t h e D N A	b a c k 5 ’ t o 3 ’ , leaving complementary	single	stranded	regions,	that	can	anneal.	This	leaves	gaps	in	the	DNA	backbone,	which are filled by the polymerase and ligase, resulting in a seamless vector	(Figure	1).	The biGBac system uses this method to assemble multiple genes	together	into	vectors. Figure	1: The	steps	of	Gibson	assembly	cloning.

There are three different levels of vectors in the biGBac system;	p L I B , pBIG1s and pBIG2s	(Figure	2,	Table	1). The	p L I B vectors store	o n e g e n e o f interest	(GOI),	adding	a	polyhedrin	promoter	and	terminator	to	generate	a	gene	expression cassette	( G E C ).	The pBIG1 vectors	h o l d u p t o 5 GECs, which are	assembled	from	PCR	fragments	with	a	set	of	overlapping	regions	labelled	α,	β,	γ,	δ,	ε	and	ω	using	Gibson	assembly.	The	pBIG2	vectors	which	hold	up	to	25	GECs,	and are made by up to five pBIG1 restriction fragments which are	a ssembled	using	the	overlapping	regions	labelled	A,	B,	C,	D,	E	and	F.	All	the	vectors	have	a	different antibiotic	resistance	gene, to help reduce background. All the vectors	can also	b e t r a n s p o s e d i n t o DH10embacY cells for bacmid production,	(hence	suitable	for	protein	production	in	insect	cells),	so	I	encourage	you	to	exploit	this	and	make	pBIG1	constructs	that	should	form	useful,	stable	sub-complexes. To	assemble	pBIG1	vectors,	the	vector	is	linearised	using	digestion	with	the	SwaI	enzyme,	leaving	blunts	ends,	with	one	end	having	the	α	assembly	overlap	region and the other end having the	β	region.	P C R i s	t h e n performed using a	different set of primers for each different pLIB	G O I. Each primer has a region	that	is	homologous	to	the	pLIB	vector	and	a	region	that	adds	to	double	stranded	overlap	for	assembly;	α,	β,	γ,	δ,	ε	or	ω	(Figure	3).	In	addition,	all	reverse	primers,	and the first forward primer,	CasI_for, have a SwaI restriction enzyme site,	hence the assembled vector should have a SwaI site between every GEC	s u c h Figure	2:	The	vectors	of	the	biGBac	system.	A:	pLIB	vectors	contain	one	gene	of	interest	(GOI)	cloned	under	the	control	of	a	polH	promoter	and	terminator	to	make	a	gene	expression	cassette	(GEC).	B:	pBIG1 vectors can store up to 5 GECs, which are assembled by Gibson assembly with overlapping	regions added by PCR. C: pBIG2 vectors can store up to 25 GECs, assembled from up to 5 pBIG1	vectors,	with	overlapping	regions	provided	in	the	vectors.

that the finally assembly can be screened using diagnostic digest with SwaI.	Primers pairs are chosen to ensure assembly overlaps are made between	adjacent	genes	and	the	vector,	for	example	the	first	gene	DNA	fragment	has	an	α	assembly overlap added to the 5’ to overlap with the vector, and a	β	t o t h e 3 ’ . The	second	gene	has	a	β	over lap	added	to	the	5’	to	over lap	with	the	fir st	gene	and	a	γ	to	the	3’	to	overlap	with	the	next	gene.	The	final	gene	has	a	ω	at	the	3’	to	overlap	with	the	vector	(Figure	2).	In	addition,	pBIG1	vectors	each	have	another	set	of	overlapping	regions	on	either	side	of	the	GECs,	labelled	A,	B,	C,	D,	E	or	F.	These have flanking PmeI sites, such that digesting pBIG1 vectors with PmeI	produces	a	DNA	fragment	with	A,	B,	C,	D,	E	or	F	on	the	5’	and	3’	ends,	which	in	turn	allow	assembly	overlaps	with	the	pBIG2	vectors. Depending	on	which	pBIG1	vector	you	used,	this	digest	product	will	have	the	regions,	A,	B,	C,	D,	E	or	F	on	the	end.	All	pBIG2	vectors	have	the	overlap	region	A,	but	vary	in	the	second	region.	For	example,	pBIG2ab	has	overlap	A	and	C,	hence	you	can	assemble	a	fragment	from	pBIG1a	and	1b.	Vector	pBIG2abc	has	overlap	A	and	D,	hence	you	can	assemble	pBIG1a,	1b	and	1c.	In	the	pBIG2	vectors,	and	in	pBIG1 vectors between the	ω	a n d t h e B , C , D , E o r F r e g i o n s , t h e r e i s a P a c I	restriction	site,	hence	pBIG2	assembly	can	be	checked	with	diagnostic	digestion	with	PacI.	Hence, the system can just be thought of as a set of Gibson assembly	homology regions that allow DNA fragment assembly and contain restriction	enzyme	sites	to	release	DNA	fragments	and	screen	for	correct	assemblies. Figure	3: The	structure	of	the	biGBac	primers.	The	blue	regions	are	homologous	to	the	region outside the GEC of the pLIB vector and are the regions that anneal to the pLIB	vectors	in	PCR.	The	red	part	of	the	sequence	are	the	Gibson	assembly	regions	that	are	added	to	the	GEC	during	PCR.	SwaI	sites	are	also	added	using	all	the	reverse	primers	and	the	first	forward	primer.

Practical	Aspects	of	the	biGBac	System	Cloning in this system	is not always straightforward, as the probability of	multiple DNA fragments assembling correctly goes down the more fragments	you try to assemble	t o g e t h e r.	This	can go	wrong	substantially	in two ways: 1)	formation of	partially assembled products, where one or two genes gets	assembled, but not all of them, or	2) formation of	empty vectors.	In	our	experience three gene assemble	well, assembling	f o u r w i l l r e q u i r e a l o t o f screening,	and	I	wouldn’t	recommend	trying	to	assemble	5	genes	in	one	go	if	you	can	avoid	it.	All	genes	will	not	behave	the	same	in	the	system,	for	example	it	can	be harder to clone	large (>8kb)	g e n e s t o g e t h e r, especially with	other genes	o f very	different	size.	In	practice,	using	diagnostic	digest	with	SwaI	and	PacI	can	be	very time consuming,	a s i t requires an overnight culture. If you don’t	p i c k t h e right colony for your	o v e r n i g h t c u l t u r e , y o u h a v e t o w a i t t o h a v e a n o t h e r g o . Some members	in the lab have had to screen more than 40 colonies to find a	fully assembled clone, wasting a lot of time and reagents.	To get over this,	we	have	introduced another screening step using	c o l o n y P C R. This uses	f o u r primers	(Table	2,	primers	S1A-D	for	pBIG1s	and	S2A-D	for	pBIG2s),	where	two	primers bind the vector and two primers bind each fragments. These primers	will produce a different sized PCR product across the vector-fragment,	fragment-fragment	and	fragment-vector	junctions;	hence	colonies	where	two	or	more genes have been assembled	will have three bands (Figure	4).	Colonies	with	empty	vector,	however	will	only	yield	one	band.	The	primers	are	different	for	pBIG1	and	pBIG2	assemblies	but	in	both	work	using	the	same	principal.	Colony PCR is a very quick reaction and makes it possible to screen many	more	colonies,	without	having	to	wait	for	an	overnight	culture,	however	if	you	have three or more genes being assembled, it may not be able to discriminate	between two or three (or more) genes being assembled. H e n c e , i n p r a c t i c e , screening	with	both	colony	PCR	and	diagnostic	digest	gives	the	highest	chance	of	success. Figure 4: C o l o n y P C R f o r s c r e e n i n g p B I G 1 c o n s t r u c t s . A : T w o p r i m e r s b i n d	t h e p B I G 1 v e c t o r , f a c i n g towards	the	fragments,	two	primers	bind	the	fragments,	facing	the	vector.	This	results	in	three	products	across the assembly junctions, of 230 bp, 380 bp and 458bp, corresponding to vector-fragment 1,	fragment 1-fragment 2 (and fragment 2-fragment 3, etc) and the last fragment	–vector. B: The empty	vector	will	only	product	one	PCR	product,	of	~350	bp.	C:	Example	of	colony	PCR	2%	agarose	gel;	the	red	+	is	a	positive	control	pBIG1	from	a	previous	cloning,	red	–	is	the	pBIG1a	empty	vector	and	colony	7,	8,	9	and	11	proved	be	correctly	assembled.

A	feature	that	is	built	in	this	system	that	isn’t	immediately	obvious,	is	that	the	Cas primers’ Gibson assembly	overlaps to assemble the pBIG1 vectors are	actually the same as to assemble the	p B I G 2 . T h a t i s,	o v e r l a p p i n g r e g i o ns	β=C,	γ=D,	δ=E	and	ε=F.	This	can	be	useful	if	you	want	to	avoid	making	a	pBIG1	with	just one gene in it. For example, imagine if you had complex made of a large	scaffold protein,	in addition to	a stable heterodimer and	a	heterotrimer	( 6 subunits	in	total).	It	would	make	sense	to	have	the	heterodimer	in	pBIG1a	and	the hetrotrimer in pBIG1b, so you can express these subcomplexes	s e p a r a t e l y.	You could	place	the scaffold protein in pBIG1c in order to make a pBIG2abc	construct with the scaffold protein, hetrodimer and hetrotrimer,	but you don’t	have to. Instead you can add the C and D Gibson assembly regions with PCR	using	CasII_for	and	CasIII_rev. This will remove one	P a c I s c r e e n i n g s i t e , b u t diagnostic digest with SwaI and PacI should still be able to identify a unique	restriction	pattern. All	the	pBIG2	vectors	start	with	the	A	assembly	overlap,	so	what	do	you	do	if	you want to make combinations of subcomplexes	that lack pBIG1a? That is,	using	the	above	example,	what	would	I	do	if	I	wanted	to	make	a	construct	that	had	the	scaffold	and	the	heterodimer	(combine	pBIG1a	and	pBIG1c)	and	another	construct that had the scaffold and the hetrotrimer (combine pBIG1b and	pBIG1c)?	You	can	make	these	constructs	by	digesting	the	empty	pBIG1	vectors	with	PmeI	and	use	the	product	as	a	linker.	For	example,	to	combine	pBIG1a	and	pBIG1c, simply digest pBIG1b, and you will have	a	4 0 0 bp linker	w i t h t h e B overlap at the 5’ end and the C overlap at the 3’ end.	This is implied by	Weissmann	et al in supplementary	Table	4,	which states that some pBIG2	constructs	contain	empty	pBIG1	vectors. Method Constructs	First	you	need	the	biGBac	vectors,	they	are	available	on	addgene:	https://www.addgene.org/kits/peters-bigbac/	Next you need to logically design your constructs. As said above, put stable	sub-complexes	in	individual	pBIG1	vectors	and	try	not	to	put	more	than	3	or	4	genes per pBIG1 vector. I computationally build all constructs I want to	using	the	program	APE	(A	Plasmid	Editor): http://biologylabs.utah.edu/jorgensen/wayned/ape/ After building	them, I perform computational digests	with	SwaI and PacI,	such	that	I	can	ensure	two	products	won’t	run	at	the	same	size	in	both	digests.	I have all	c o n s t r u c ts ordered	or	subcloned	lacking restriction enzyme sites	used	for	subsequent	steps	of	biGBac	cloning,	ie	PmeI,	SwaI,	PacI,	and	any	other	restriction	sites	for	downstream	cloning. pBIG1	Assembly:	PCR	each	pLIB	expression	cassette	(a	promoter,	gene	and	terminator)	using	the	Cas	primers	in	primer	Table	2.	Each	Cas	primer	will	add	a	sequence	(α,	β,	γ,

etc)	to	the	5’	and	3’	end	of	the	gene	expression	cassette,	which	can	be	used	for	assembly.	The	first	gene	should	use	CasI_for,	and	CasI_rev,	the	second	CasII_for	and	CasII_rev	a n d t h e f i n a l , u s i n g Casω_rev, with the forward version of the	second to last reverse primer. I use primers from Integrated DNA Technology	with standard de-salting purification (Weissmann used PAGE purified	oligonucleotides). (If you are sub-cloning	with	Gibson	assembly,	prior	to	running	gel	extraction,	add	1μL	of	DpnI	enzyme	and	incubate	at	37°C	for	an	hour,	this	will	remove	plasmid	template.) • You can also use this protocol to amplify the pBIG1 vectors using the	primers	alpha_rev	and	omega_for	from	primer	table	2,	but	in	this	case	a	DpnI	digest	is	essential. Digest	Vector	While	the	PCR	is	going	on,	digest	the	pBIG1	vector	(s)	to	be	used	with	SwaI. Mini	prep	DNA	(10μg) 20-30μL	10x	buffer	3.1 4	μL	SwaI	enzyme 1-2μL	Water Up	to	40μL • Incubate overnight at room temperature (incubation at higher	temperatures	inactivates	SwaI).	In	the	morning	add	a	further	1μL	of	enzyme,	and	incubate for a further hour before inactivating at 65°C for 20 minutes. It is	essential	the	vectors	are	well	cut,	or	you	will	have	a	high	background. • Gel-extract vector	and	P C R p r o d u c t i n	a 1%	agarose gel.	I w o u l d recommend	running	uncut	pBIG1	vector	on	the	same	gel,	such	that	you	can	see	the	band	has	shifted	completely	on	digestion.	Use	the	zymo	gel	extraction	kit	to	purify DNA, as this kit results in very clean and concentrated DNA, which will	help the Gibson assembly reaction proceed efficiently. DNA fragment for	purification	is	greater	than	8kb,	adding	equal	gel	volume	of	water	will	improve	DNA yield. Elute in 10uL of water and quantify DNA concentration	using	nanodrop. Zymo	kit:	https://www.bioscience.co.uk/search/132097/

Assembly	Reaction	I	had	used	both	the	following	kits	successfully:	https://www.neb.com/products/e5510-gibson-assembly-cloning-kit#Product%20Information	https://www.neb.com/products/e5520-nebuilder-hifi-dna-assembly-cloning-kit#Product%20Information	You can make your own	like	Weissmann	et al, but the kits are a nice	entry-level	way	of	cloning	with	Gibson	assembly.	Although the kit recommends using 10μL of 2x assembly mix with 10μL of	DNA	mix,	I	find	5μL	of	each	works	fine.	The	first	time	you	use	the	kit,	defrost	it	slowly	on	ice,	spin	down	condensation,	make	5μL	aliquots	on	ice	and	freeze	until	required.	I	use	PCR	tubes	and	use	a	PCR	machine	for	the	assembly	reaction. Mix	on	ice.	• Vector:	(pBIG1a,	1b,	etc)	50-100ng	• Inserts:	5	fold	molar	excess	for	inserts	smaller	than	the	vector	and	a	2	fold	excess	for	inserts	of	similar	of	larger	size	(4kb	or	bigger).	• Water	to	5μL	Add	this	to	a	5μL	aliquot	of	2x	assembly	mix. • Incubate	at	50°C	for	15-60	minutes.	(15	minutes	is	fine	for	two	fragment	assembly,	but	more	fragments	require	longer). • Transform	2μL	of	assembly	into	20μL	of	cells	that	come	with	the	kit	(any	highly competent cells for cloning purposes should be fine), plate	onto	amp+spec	LB	plates	and	grow	over	night	at	37°C.	I	like	to	do	a	control	using	an	equivalent	amount	of	vector	without	assembly	mix	to	give	an	idea	of	how	many	background	colonies	there	may	be.	For	the	first	assembly	reaction	you	ever do, you could also use the assembly control provided with the Gibson	assembly	kit	to	ensure	your	assembly	mix	works	as	expected. Screening	by	colony	PCR	Hopefully	your	transformation	plates	have	~30	or	more	colonies.	I’ve designed a set of 4 primers	( S 1 A-D)	f o r s c r e e n i n g with colony PCR	whether	assembly	has	occurred.	When	all	primers	are	used	for	a	PCR	reaction,	this results	i n t h r e e p r o d u c t s i f a ssembly has been successful, but only one of	size	350bp	if	no	insert	has	assembled	(figure	4).	Partial	assemblies	are	possible,	so all three bands need to be present. I find screening at least 5 colonies of	assembly	reaction	is	advisable,	if	you	assemble	more	than	3	genes,	or	the	genes	are variable sizes, I would recommend you screen as many as practical (using	strip	PCR	tubes	or	plates	means	this	can	be	high	through-put). I	use	the	KAPPA	robust	PCR	kit,	because	it	always	work	for	me:	https://www.n-genetics.com/file/KAPA2G_Robust_TDS_KR0379_v7.16.pdf • Leave	transformation	plates	until	colonies	are	a	reasonable	size.

• Circle and number the colonies you wish to screen and pick them into	80μL of sterile water	w i t h a p i p e t t e t i p, being careful not to scope up any	agar	as	this	can	lead	to	false	positive.	Don’t	pick	up	too	much	colony,	as	the	PCR	won’t	work.	The	water	solution	should	not	be	cloudy. PCR	mix	: 1x 10x	dNTPs	(10	mM) 0.2	μL 2	μL	primer	mix	(10	μM	of	each) 0.5	μL 5	μL	5x	Buffer	B 2	μL 20	μL	Kappa	robust	enzyme 0.1	μL 1	μL	water 6.2	μL 62	μL • Mix	on	ice,	aliquot	9μL	per	tube,	then	add	1μL	of	colony	water.	• Use	annealing	temperature	of	58°C	and	an	extension	time	of	30s,	for	30-35	cycles. • Run	PCR	product	on	a	2%	gel	and	check	band	pattern.	• Set up over-night cultures for mini-preps of 3	or 4	colonies which	resulted	in	correct	three	bands. Diagnostic	digest:	To determine if all genes have been assembled, perform a diagnostic digest	with	SwaI. This will	cut between all the expression GECs	s o y o u s h o u l d g e t a DNA	band	for	each	of	your	genes,	where	each	will	be	the	size	of	your	gene	plus	about	500bp.	(I	make	a	plasmid	map	of	what	I	expect	to	make	using	the	program	APE	(A	Plasmid	Editor),	a	get	a	predicted	band	pattern	for	digestion	with	SwaI:	http://biologylabs.utah.edu/jorgensen/wayned/ape/	). Mini	prep	DNA 4μL	10x	buffer 1μL	water 4.5μL	SwaI 0.5μL • Incubate for a couple of hours at room temperature and run on 1% gel.	Shorter	digests	are	possible,	but	if	digest	is	incomplete,	the	resultant	DNA	gel	can	be	very	hard	to	interpret	(you	will	get	extra	bands). If	you	have	very	low	efficiency,	with	mainly	partially	assembled	products,	see	if you can find a pattern in what is going wrong. If one band is frequently	missing,	t r y add more of that during the assembly reaction. You can also try	change	the	order	of	your	genes,	which	seems	to	help	if	genes	are	very	different	sizes. If band pattern is correct, proceed to	pBIG2 assembly.	At this point you can	also	send	your	pBIG1	constructs	for	sequencing.	I	typically	use	biGBac	to	make	5-10 constructs at once and my genes are huge, so I tend to test two or three	different	constructs	for	expression	and	confirm	the	sequence	by	mass	spec	and	sequencing after a construct	shows good expression. This saves sequencing	several	20kb	constructs	that	may	not	even	express.

Assembly	of	pBIG2	constructs	• Digest pBIG1s and pBIG2s	with	PmeI. Digesting the pBIG1 assemblies	with	PmeI	also	acts	as	a	screening	step,	so	ensure	you	check	the	band	size	is	what	you	expect. Mini	prep	(5-10μg) 20-30μL	10x	cutsmart	buffer 4	μL	PmeI	enzyme 1-2μL	Water Up	to	50μL • Incubate at 37°C for a few hours for pBIG1 vectors, and overnight for	pBIG2	vectors. • Run 1% gel, check that band formed by	PmeI	d i g e s t i s t h e e x p e c t e d s i z e for the genes you have assembled, using the APE program then	g el extract	using	the	zymo	kit,	eluting	in	10μL	of	water. • Perform	assembly	as	above,	this	time	plating	on	Amp+Cam	plates. Screening	by	colony	PCR	• Screen	as	above	using	second	set	(S2A-D)	of	screening	primers.	These	will	result	in	424,	322	&	680	bp	products	if	assembly	has	occurred	or	800	bp	if	no	insert	is	present. Diagnostic	digest	• Grow over nights for mini-preps, and perform a diagnostic digest	with	PacI. This cuts out each fragment assembled in to pBIG2 vectors. You can	also check using a SwaI digest, which will cut out each of	y o u r g e n e expression cassettes. This can result in a lot of bands, so I normal do	diagnostic	digests	with	both	enzymes	separately	to	check	everything	is	there. Expression	in	Insect	cells	After you have	t h e biGBac constructs, standard insect cells protocols apply.	Transform your	pLIB, pBIG1 or pBIG2 constructs into DH10emBacY cells, and	purify	the	bacmid. Make	P1	virus	stock	by	transfecting	the	Bacmid	into	Sf9	cells,	after	3	days	amplify	the	virus	by	adding	transfection	supernanant	to	make	a	P2	virus	stock	for	expression.	Be	aware	that	if	you	have	a	large	construct	(>20kb)	the	P2	may	take	longer	than	usual.	You	should	also	take	extra	care	of	your	cells	to	make	sure	they	don’t	over	grow	between	passages,	as	this	can	greatly	effect	protein	expression	especially	for	large	complexes. Discussion Construct	Design Construct	design	is	really	important	with	biGBac	cloning.	I	encourage	you	to	think	about	all	the	ways	you	might	want	to	use	your	constructs	before	you	start.

Things to consider are do you just want the whole complex, or are there sub-complexes you may also want to investigate? Has this complex been purified	before	so	you	know	where	to	put	the	tags?	Chances	are	you	will	have	to	change	this as you optimise your purification or perform some other down stream	experiment. To prevent having to go through multi-fragment assembly again	and again, I suggest you	think about making every pBIG1 vector a usable sub-complex and make any tags used removable at a DNA level using flanking	unique	restriction	enzyme	sites.	You	can	also	put	a	unique	restriction	site	where	you	may	want	to	add	a	tag,	such	that	adding	the	tag	is	as	easy	as	digesting	the	pBIG1 or pBIG2 assembled	vector and using Gibson assembly to add the tag	sequence. Although I haven’t rigorously tested different types of tags, some	repetitive sequence tags seem to make the cloning slightly more	c h a l l e n g i n g . Hence, there is logic in making	c o n s t r u c t s w i t h o u t a f f i n i t y t a g s a n d j u s t restriction	sites,	then	add	a	range	of	different	tags	in	a	systematic	way. It may also be the case you want	make a whole gene removable and	exchangeable, for example if you want to	make a series of mutations in a	catalytic	site	or	similar.	To	do	this	you	simply	have	to	add	a	unique	restriction	enzyme site in	t h e Cas primers between the pLIB homology region and the	variable	region. As the restriction sites cannot be present in any of	your genes, or in the	pBIG1s	or	pBIG2s,	you	won’t	have	a	lot	of	choice,	so	this	requires	thought	before	ordering	the	genes.	I	used	XbaI,	NdeI,	SpeI,	KasI	and	XhoI	for	these	purposes	as	I	had	these	enzymes	at	hand. The	largest	source	of	false	positives	is	from	incomplete	digestion	of	vectors.	This	is	a	particular	problem	for	pBIG1	vectors	as	SwaI	enzyme	which	linearises	it cuts at room temperature and is inactivated at higher temperatures.	Weissmann do partially address this problem, by performing a long digest,	adding	the	enzyme	in	two	separate	rounds.	An	alternative	way	to	linearise	the	vector is by PCR	( u s i n g p rimers	alpha_rev and omega_for	i n t a b l e 2), then	remove the vector template by	DpnI digestion (will remove any DNA purified	from	E.	coli)	and	gel	extraction.	The	yield	for	this	typically	is	not	great	and	does	come will a small risk of backbone mutation, but using this method I get no	vector	background.	Doing	backbone	PCR	also	enables	further	modification	of	the	system.	The	overlapping	regions	(α,	A,	β,	B,	γ,	etc)	were	chosen	by	Weissmann	based	on computational optimisation to prevent secondary structure and lack cross	complementarily, but they never actually test whether their algorithm for	choosing	the	overlaps	performed	better	than	a	random	piece	of	DNA	~25bp	long	or	test	whether	longer	pieces	of	DNA	might	be	more	efficient.	Given	Gibson	et	al	(Gibson	et	al	2010)	were	able	to	assemble	a	1.08	Mega	base	bacterial	genome,	assembling	10	fragments	at	a	time,	the	sequence	of	the	overlaps	should	not	be	so	sensitive	and	5	fragments	should	not	produce	such	low	efficiency.	Companies	such	as	DNA	technology	at	Synthetic	genomes	incorporated,	for	which	Daniel	G.	Gibson	is	the	Vice	president,	suggest	overlaps	of	≥40	bp	if	you	want	to	assemble	5 genes, especially if those genes are over 8	kb.	Hence, 5-fragment	biGBac	assembly could be more efficient if the overlaps were extended.	As the pBIG1	assembly is mediated by overlaps introduced by	PCR,	these overlaps could

easily be extended by just lengthening the PCR primer. The vector overlaps	could	also	be	lengthened	by	linearising	the	vector	using	PCR. Alternatively, as	t h e biGBac system is a set of Gibson assembly homology	regions	that	allow	DNA	fragment	assembly	and	contain	restriction	enzyme	sites	to	release	DNA	fragments	and	screen	for	correct	assemblies,	this	concept	could	be further extended to make another	pBIG vector. Additional level of	concatenation is possible by incorporating an additional blunt cutting enzyme	site flanking Gibson assembly overlaps in the vector of the pBIG1s and adding	another	screening	restriction	enzyme	site	(Figure	5).	This	must	be	coupled	with	minor	changes	in	th e Cas	primers	to	ensure	Gibson	assembly	overlaps	are	still	complementary, but by using this approach 27 genes could be assembled	w i t h only	three	fragments	being	assembled	at	a	time.	This	would	add	two	days	to	the	6	day	protocol,	but	is	likely	to	have	a	higher	efficiency. Conclusion	The	biGBac system is a great modular way of making a large amount of	expression	constructs	for	complex	molecular	assemblies.	By	fully	understanding	all	of	the	features,	I	hope	you	can	see	how	this	could	be	adapted	and	extended. Figure	5:	Introducing	a	third	assembly	step	could	be	achieved	by	modifying	the	overlapping	regions	in	pBIG1	assembly	to	include	a	new	blunt	cutting	enzyme	site	(eg	SmaI)	for	cassette	removal	and	a	new	enzyme	site	for	screening	(KasI).	These	overlaps	would	have	to	be	added	to	both	GECs	from	pLIB	and	the	pBIG1	vectors,	which	could	be	achieved	by	PCR.	After	the	first	round	of	assembly,	digestion	with	SmaI	would	release	the	cassette	allowing	an	additional	step	on	assembly	into	another	vector	based	off	pBIG1. As the PmeI sites would still be present in this modified pBIG1, DNA fragments from PmeI	digest	could	be	assembled	in	pBIG2s.
